strengths: The paper relaxes the classical smoothness condition to the generalized smoothness condition.
Furthermore, the convergence guarantee is competitive and matches the SOTA.

The authors present the first analysis of normalized error feedback algorithms in a distributed setting for minimizing non-convex objectives satisfying generalized smoothness conditions. The proposed algorithm matches the guarantees of the standard error feedback algorithms under classical smoothness assumptions.
The authors also show convergence under the stochastic settings.
The authors numerically evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm.

The paper clearly articulates the limitations of previous approaches and their constraints in proof, while explicitly highlighting the improvements and increased generalizability introduced by the proposed method.
This paper presents the first convergence proof for normalized error feedback algorithms under generalized smoothness in a decentralized setting, filling an existing theoretical gap on this issue.
The proof appears to follow a standard framework for decentralized problems, making it fairly credible.
The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The notation definitions are clear.
The theorems are clear and complete. The theoretical results are novel and seem to be sound.
weaknesses: The only notable contribution is the relaxation from the classical smoothness condition to the generalized smoothness condition, and the analysis is known from Chen et al. 2023 and various other works, so the theoretical analysis is not too impressive.
The empirical settings are a bit limited and not well-motivated.
The paper does not present well the communication aspect of the algorithm, nor its proof idea.

The discussion on the requirement of heterogeneity assumption by the earlier algorithms and the proposed algorithm not requiring the assumption is slightly misleading; the authors should clarify the connection between their single local update approach and the lack of heterogeneity assumptions, and discuss performance with multiple local updates.
Why both Assumptions 1 and 2 are required? Assumption 2 implies Assumption 1, and the authors should justify the inclusion of both assumptions or revise the analysis to rely only on Assumption 1.

For the stochastic setting, the presented analysis does not capture the effect of the number of clients on performance; the authors should analyze or discuss whether the proposed algorithm achieves linear speed-up with the number of clients.
In Theorem 1, is there an upper bound on the requirement of γ₀? Why such a bound is not necessary for Theorem 1 but is required in Theorem 2?

The presented numerical results are very weak; the authors have only compared against the EF21 algorithm and should compare with several federated baselines such as FedAvg, CHOCO-SGD, momentum based algorithms, etc.
The algorithm itself does not present significant innovation, as it primarily combines the standard EF21 with a normalization technique.

The technical novelty appears limited; the proof primarily combines existing tools on (L₀,L₁)-smoothness, error feedback, and analysis of normalized gradient descent with momentum, which are well-established techniques, and the results, while solid, are not particularly surprising.

I am not sure why Theorem 2 implies the results of NSGD-M as the author mentioned in line 406; there is a mismatch that when σ=0, i.e. the deterministic case, the order of Theorem 2 is still O(T^{-1/4}), while Theorem 1 in (Cutkosky & Mehta, 2020) is O(T^{-1/2}). The authors should consider following (Cutkosky & Mehta, 2020) to allow a step size order shift regarding the magnitude of σ to fix this.
